case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Supreme Court should approve and enter the States’ proposed consent decree settling Rio Grande Compact disputes when the United States (an intervenor) objects that the decree impairs federal Reclamation Project interests and would effectively bind the United States without its consent, and whether the United States’ remaining claims should be dismissed from the Court’s original-jurisdiction case without prejudice.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. III, § 2, cl. 2; 28 U.S.C. § 1251(a) (exclusive original jurisdiction over controversies between States) and § 1251(b)(2) (nonexclusive original jurisdiction over United States v. State); Rio Grande Compact, Act of May 31, 1939, ch. 155, 53 Stat. 785; Reclamation Act of 1902, ch. 1093, 32 Stat. 388 (as amended); McCarran Amendment, 43 U.S.C. § 666.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Texas (joined by New Mexico and Colorado in seeking entry of the decree) argues that the negotiated consent decree is a valid Compact-compliance settlement that resolves the interstate apportionment dispute consistent with the Rio Grande Compact and with federal Reclamation law, including accounting for the effects of post-Compact groundwater pumping; that entering the decree appropriately ends the States’ compact controversy within the Court’s exclusive original jurisdiction; and that any remaining federal complaints about in-state Project operations and intrastate administration can be pursued by the United States in other forums (federal district court or state adjudications under the McCarran Amendment), so the United States should not be permitted to leverage its intervention to block a state-to-state compact settlement.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States (as intervenor aligned in part with Texas’s original theory) objects to entry of the consent decree on the ground that it would impose or alter federal obligations and/or impair federal contract and Reclamation Project interests without the United States’ consent, contrary to principles that a consent decree cannot bind a nonconsenting sovereign; it contends New Mexico’s Compact obligations include a duty not to interfere with operation of the Rio Grande Project below Elephant Butte (including impacts from groundwater pumping and other diversions) and seeks relief broad enough to protect Project supplies not only to Texas but also within New Mexico; and it argues the Court should retain and adjudicate those federal claims in the original action rather than dismissing them as merely intrastate disputes relegated to other fora.

John Roberts.reasoning: The States’ best point remains the formal one Justice Thomas identifies: in our exclusive original jurisdiction, we could enter a State-to-State decree while disclaiming any binding effect on the United States. But Justice Kagan is right to press Firefighters v. Cleveland’s practical-effect rule—if the decree effectively restructures Rio Grande Project operations or accounting, it impermissibly impairs a nonconsenting intervenor sovereign’s asserted claims regardless of labels. Texas v. New Mexico (2018), as Justice Barrett emphasizes, cuts against sidelining the United States after we recognized its distinct, project-linked interests as properly before us in this original action. The legitimacy-preserving, narrow course is to deny entry as drafted (or require modifications that avoid prejudicing federal claims) and to retain the United States’ remaining claims rather than using a consent decree as an end run around unresolved federal issues.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The opposing side’s best argument—that our exclusive original jurisdiction permits a States-only consent decree while merely disclaiming any effect on the United States—fails because a decree’s legal force turns on its practical operation, not its labels. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, if the decree functionally directs or constrains Rio Grande Project accounting and operations, it effectively adjudicates federal statutory interests without federal consent, which Article III and § 1251(a) do not authorize. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Firefighters v. Cleveland reinforces that we may not approve a consent decree that imposes obligations on or disposes of the valid claims of a nonconsenting intervenor sovereign, and Texas v. New Mexico (2018) confirms the United States has distinct, properly joined interests here that cannot be sidelined to facilitate settlement. Nothing in the constitutional text, the Compact, or Reclamation law supplies authority for this Court to restructure federal duties via a “consent” instrument to which the United States does not agree.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The States’ best argument remains that, given our exclusive original jurisdiction, we can enter a States-only settlement and add language disclaiming any effect on the United States. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, a decree of this Court has unavoidable real-world force, and under Firefighters v. Cleveland we look to practical effect, not labels—if the decree functionally dictates Rio Grande Project operations or accounting, it impermissibly imposes obligations on a nonconsenting sovereign and prejudices its claims. Justice Barrett’s invocation of Texas v. New Mexico (2018) further supports keeping the United States’ distinct, properly pleaded Project-related claims in this action rather than neutralizing them to facilitate a settlement. On a textualist, institution-protective view, we should deny entry as drafted (or require revisions that genuinely avoid operational constraints) and proceed to adjudicate the remaining federal claims.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The States’ best argument—that our exclusive original jurisdiction lets us enter a States-only decree while the United States litigates elsewhere—fails because a consent decree’s legality turns on its practical effect, not a formal nonbinding label. Justice Kagan’s Firefighters framing is decisive for me: if the decree functionally dictates Rio Grande Project accounting and operations, it would impair a nonconsenting sovereign intervenor’s live claims, which we cannot do by “consent.” Texas v. New Mexico (2018) also matters; as Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, we already recognized the United States’ distinct project-linked stake within this very original action, so sidelining those claims would be both institutionally improper and risky for downstream communities depending on lawful Project administration. I therefore would deny entry as drafted (or require modifications that cure the federal objections) and would not dismiss the United States’ remaining claims in a way that prejudices them.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The States’ best point remains that we could enter a purely state-to-state settlement while disclaiming any effect on the United States, but as Chief Justice Roberts stresses we have to judge a consent decree by its practical operation, not its labels. Firefighters v. Cleveland makes that constraint dispositive: if the decree would effectively dictate Rio Grande Project accounting/operations and thereby impair the United States’ asserted Reclamation-based interests, we cannot treat it as a harmless consensual resolution over a nonconsenting intervenor’s objection. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Texas v. New Mexico (2018) reinforces the statutory-coherence and workability problem—having recognized distinct federal project-linked interests as properly in this original action, it would be incoherent to enter an enforceable decree that functionally cabins those interests while purporting not to bind them. I therefore would deny entry as drafted and retain the United States’ remaining claims for merits resolution unless and until the United States joins a settlement or those claims are adjudicated.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The States’ best argument is that our exclusive original jurisdiction over controversies between States permits us to enter a States-only settlement while disclaiming any effect on federal interests, but that is formalism that cannot overcome a consent decree’s practical operation. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, Firefighters v. Cleveland requires us to ask whether the decree would in substance dispose of or prejudice a nonconsenting intervenor’s valid claims; here the United States plausibly alleges the decree would restructure Rio Grande Project accounting and operations grounded in federal law. Justice Thomas’s separation-of-powers point reinforces, on an originalist reading of Article III and § 1251(a), that our jurisdiction to resolve state disputes does not supply authority to adjudicate or effectively command federal statutory duties via a “consent” instrument lacking federal consent. Texas v. New Mexico (2018) cuts against dismissing or sidelining the federal claims because we already recognized the United States’ distinct project-related interests as properly joined in this very original action.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The States’ best point remains that we can enter a States-only decree while expressly disclaiming any binding effect on the United States, but as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, labels cannot overcome practical operation: a decree that dictates Project accounting and deliveries will predictably constrain federal Reclamation administration and thus prejudice federal interests. Justice Kagan’s Firefighters v. Cleveland framing is decisive under my institutionalist approach—consent decrees cannot impose obligations on or dispose of the valid claims of a nonconsenting intervenor sovereign, and this record shows a serious risk of exactly that. Justice Barrett’s reminder that Texas v. New Mexico (2018) recognized the United States’ distinct, properly joined interests underscores that we should not use a consent instrument in an original action to effectively sideline federal claims without adjudication or federal consent. The legitimacy- and precedent-respecting course is to deny entry as drafted (or require federal participation/modifications that truly preserve federal rights) and retain the United States’ remaining claims for merits resolution.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The States’ best argument remains that our exclusive original jurisdiction under Article III and 28 U.S.C. § 1251(a) permits entry of a state-to-state decree notwithstanding federal objections, so long as we disclaim any binding effect on the United States. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the operative question is practical effect: if the decree would in substance channel Rio Grande Project accounting and operations, a disclaimer cannot prevent it from prejudicing the United States’ asserted interests. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Firefighters v. Cleveland reinforces that a consent decree cannot impose obligations on or dispose of the valid claims of a nonconsenting intervenor, and Texas v. New Mexico (2018) counsels against treating the federal claims as collateral once we have recognized them as properly joined in this original action. On a textualist and precedent-respecting view, § 1251(a) allocates forum; it does not expand our power to adjudicate federal rights through a consent instrument lacking federal consent, so we should deny entry as drafted (or require revisions that avoid any practical impairment) and retain the federal claims for merits resolution.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The States’ strongest move is the formalist one: enter a decree resolving only state-to-state duties while declaring it nonbinding on the United States. But as Justice Kagan stresses under Firefighters v. Cleveland, we have to look to practical effect, and here the decree’s accounting and operational provisions would predictably function as a command that constrains Reclamation’s administration of the Project and effectively prejudices the United States’ live claims. Chief Justice Roberts’s institutional point reinforces my procedural-fairness concern: we should not use a consent instrument to moot or sideline a nonconsenting sovereign intervenor’s properly joined interests that Texas v. New Mexico (2018) said are entitled to be heard in this very original action. Given the real-world consequences and the incomplete process for federal objections, I would deny entry as drafted and retain the federal claims for merits resolution unless and until the United States consents or the decree is reworked to avoid these functional constraints.

John Roberts.reasoning: A consent decree rests on the parties’ consent and may not impose obligations on, or dispose of the claims of, a nonconsenting intervenor sovereign; approving the States’ proposed decree over the United States’ objection would risk effectively binding federal Reclamation Project interests without federal consent. Under Firefighters v. Cleveland, a court may enter a decree over an intervenor’s objection only so long as it does not purport to settle or extinguish the intervenor’s valid claims, and here the United States plausibly asserts the decree would impair its Project-related interests and alter federal operational obligations. Given the Court’s institutional interests and the limits of our Art. III original jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1251, the narrower course is to decline to enter the decree as presently drafted and to avoid dismissing the United States’ remaining claims from this original action where they are intertwined with the Compact dispute recognized in Texas v. New Mexico (2018).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III and 28 U.S.C. § 1251(a) grant this Court exclusive original jurisdiction over controversies between States, but nothing in the Constitution or the Rio Grande Compact authorizes the Court to enter a consent decree that binds or alters the obligations of a nonconsenting sovereign intervenor. Under Firefighters v. Cleveland, 478 U.S. 501, 529 (1986), and consistent with United States v. Texas, 507 U.S. 529 (1993), a consent decree between some parties cannot dispose of the valid claims of a nonconsenting intervenor nor impose obligations upon it; the United States’ objection therefore bars entry of a decree that would impair federal Reclamation Project interests or effectively adjudicate federal claims without consent. Given the United States’ asserted Compact and Reclamation Act interests, its remaining claims should not be dismissed from this original action merely to reroute them to other fora, because doing so would evade the Court’s duty to resolve the properly joined controversy as framed in Texas v. New Mexico, 583 U.S. 407 (2018).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Court should not enter a consent decree over the objection of the United States where the decree would effectively dispose of the United States’ Compact/Reclamation claims or impose operational obligations on a nonconsenting sovereign, because “a court’s approval of a consent decree between some of the parties … cannot dispose of the valid claims of nonconsenting intervenors” and may not “impose[] obligations on a party that did not consent.” Local No. 93, Int’l Ass’n of Firefighters v. City of Cleveland, 478 U.S. 501, 529 (1986). That constraint has special force in an original action under Art. III and 28 U.S.C. § 1251, where the Court’s decree would carry binding effect and practical consequences for federal Reclamation Project operations under the Reclamation Act of 1902 and the Rio Grande Compact as enacted by Congress. Consistent with Texas v. New Mexico (2018), the United States’ remaining claims should not be dismissed merely to facilitate a state-to-state settlement if doing so would either prejudice federal interests or force the United States into other fora despite its proper participation here; at minimum, those claims should be retained or any dismissal must preserve full federal rights without allowing the decree to bind the United States.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: A consent decree may not "dispose of the valid claims of nonconsenting intervenors," and entering the States’ proposed decree over the United States’ objection would risk binding a sovereign and impairing asserted federal Reclamation Project interests without federal consent, contrary to Local No. 93, Int’l Ass’n of Firefighters v. City of Cleveland. The Court’s exclusive original jurisdiction under Article III and 28 U.S.C. § 1251(a) authorizes resolution of the interstate Compact controversy, but it does not justify extinguishing or effectively adjudicating the United States’ independent claims as an intervenor—especially where those claims allege interference with federal Project operations tied to the Rio Grande Compact and federal Reclamation law. Given the United States’ distinct federal responsibilities and contracts under the Reclamation Act, fairness and practical impacts counsel against approving a settlement that could diminish water deliveries and harm downstream communities reliant on Project administration. The appropriate course is to decline entry of the decree as proposed (or require modifications addressing federal objections) and not dismiss the United States’ remaining claims without prejudice from this original action if they are intertwined with Compact compliance and Project operations, consistent with Texas v. New Mexico (2018) recognizing a federal interest sufficient to support intervention in this dispute.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Our original jurisdiction under Article III and 28 U.S.C. § 1251(a) empowers us to resolve the States’ Compact controversy, but it does not authorize us to enter a “consent decree” that purports to dispose of the United States’ claims or materially impair federal Reclamation Project interests over the United States’ objection. Under Local No. 93, Int’l Ass’n of Firefighters v. Cleveland, a court may approve a settlement among some parties, but it “cannot dispose of the valid claims of nonconsenting intervenors,” and the proposed decree here functions in practical effect to bind the United States’ asserted Project-related rights without its consent. Given Texas v. New Mexico (2018) recognizing the United States’ distinct interests in Project operations within this Compact dispute, the workable course is to deny entry of a decree that prejudges those interests and to retain the federal claims for adjudication (or a settlement including the United States), rather than dismissing them from this original action without prejudice. That approach respects statutory coherence between the Rio Grande Compact and federal Reclamation law while preserving a forum capable of providing complete relief.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III and 28 U.S.C. § 1251(a) give this Court exclusive original jurisdiction over the States’ compact controversy, but nothing in that grant authorizes the Court to enter a consent decree that binds a nonconsenting sovereign or disposes of its claims. Under Local No. 93, Int’l Ass’n of Firefighters v. Cleveland, 478 U.S. 501, 529 (1986), a court may not approve a consent decree that imposes obligations on a party that did not consent or that extinguishes the valid claims of a nonconsenting intervenor; the United States’ objection that the decree would impair federal Reclamation Project interests and alter federal operational obligations therefore precludes entry as proposed. Consistent with separation-of-powers principles and the limits of consent-based adjudication, the United States’ remaining claims should not be dismissed from this original action without its agreement where they plausibly implicate federal statutory duties and property/contract interests under Reclamation law rather than merely intrastate administration. Texas v. New Mexico, 583 U.S. 407 (2018), confirms the United States may intervene to protect distinct federal interests in compact litigation, and those interests cannot be sidelined by a state-to-state settlement that would effectively bind the United States.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: A consent decree cannot be used to dispose of or effectively bind a nonconsenting intervenor’s claims, and here the United States—having been permitted to intervene in this original action—objects that the decree would impair federal Reclamation Project interests and alter the practical operation of federal obligations without federal consent. Under Local No. 93, Int’l Ass’n of Firefighters v. Cleveland, 478 U.S. 501, 529 (1986), the States may settle their own disputes, but the Court may not enter a decree that resolves or prejudices the intervenor’s valid claims; that concern is especially weighty when the intervenor is the United States administering a federal reclamation project under the Reclamation Act of 1902. Given Article III and 28 U.S.C. § 1251’s allocation of original jurisdiction, the prudent, institutionally cautious course is to decline to approve the decree over the federal objection and to retain (or at minimum not dismiss) the United States’ remaining claims so they can be adjudicated on a complete record rather than shifted piecemeal to other fora. That approach best respects precedent, preserves federal interests, and avoids entering a decree whose workability and enforceability would be compromised by ongoing federal objections.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article III and 28 U.S.C. § 1251(a) give this Court exclusive original jurisdiction to resolve the States’ Rio Grande Compact controversy, but they do not authorize entry of a “consent” decree that, by its operative terms, would determine or impair the United States’ pleaded Compact/Reclamation interests over its objection. Under Local No. 93, Int’l Ass’n of Firefighters v. Cleveland and United States v. Ward Baking Co., a consent decree is voluntary and “cannot dispose of the valid claims of nonconsenting intervenors,” and Texas v. New Mexico (2018) specifically allowed the United States to pursue the Compact claims it pleaded in this original action. Because the United States has not consented and its claims have not been adjudicated on the merits, the Court should not approve and enter the proposed decree insofar as it would effectively bind the United States, nor should it dismiss the United States’ remaining claims from the original case without prejudice.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: A consent decree cannot “impose duties or obligations on a third party, without that party’s agreement,” and a court’s approval of a settlement among some parties “cannot dispose of the valid claims of nonconsenting intervenors.” Firefighters v. Cleveland, 478 U.S. 501, 529–530 (1986). Here, the proposed decree would effectively direct federal Rio Grande Project operations and accounting and thereby bind the United States—an intervenor asserting independent Reclamation Project and Compact-related interests—without its consent, which is incompatible with those limits and with the Court’s approach in Texas v. New Mexico, 583 U.S. 407 (2018) (recognizing the United States’ entitlement to intervene to protect federal project interests). Given the procedural fairness concerns of foreclosing an intervenor’s claims via others’ settlement, I would not enter the decree over the United States’ objection and would not dismiss the United States’ remaining claims from the Court’s original-jurisdiction case on the States’ motion.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Supreme Court, in its original jurisdiction Rio Grande Compact case, should approve a Texas–New Mexico consent decree that would resolve the States’ Compact dispute while dismissing the United States’ asserted claims and avoiding any decree terms that would impose new obligations or constrain federal reclamation/project operations without the United States’ consent.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. III, § 2, cl. 2; 28 U.S.C. § 1251(a) & (b)(2); Rio Grande Compact (Act of May 31, 1939, ch. 155, 53 Stat. 785); Reclamation Act of 1902, ch. 1093, 32 Stat. 388 (as amended); McCarran Amendment, 43 U.S.C. § 666.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Texas (as the original plaintiff State) alleges New Mexico’s below-Elephant Butte groundwater pumping and related in-state actions deplete Rio Grande Project water that must reach Texas under the Compact, and therefore seeks enforceable Compact compliance that accounts for the effects of post-Compact groundwater pumping and ensures deliveries to Texas (with Colorado also implicated upstream). Texas supports resolving the interstate controversy through a consent decree that sets enforceable delivery/administration terms consistent with the Compact and federal reclamation law and that removes the federal government’s disruptive role in the Compact enforcement posture.
case_analysis.respondent_position: New Mexico (and supporting amici) argues the States’ proposed consent decree properly resolves the interstate Compact dispute at the state line and that remaining disputes about water administration and the Rio Grande Project within New Mexico are intrastate matters for other fora (e.g., state adjudications or lower federal courts under the McCarran Amendment framework). The United States, by contrast, excepts to the Special Master’s recommendation to enter the consent decree, contending the decree cannot bind or impose obligations on the federal government without its consent and that the federal government should be able to pursue its own Project-interference and contract-based theories outside the Compact-only settlement reached by the States.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point—that §1251(a) exclusivity should prevent the United States from effectively vetoing a State–State settlement—has real force, but it does not answer Firefighters v. Cleveland’s core limit on judicial power: we cannot enter a “consent” decree that, in operation, disposes of or burdens a nonconsenting intervenor’s live claims in the same case. As Justice Kagan and Justice Alito emphasize, labeling the federal dismissal “without prejudice” is not curative if the decree’s operational baselines would practically constrain Reclamation or predetermine the United States’ Compact-related positions recognized as cognizable in Texas v. New Mexico (2018). I agree with Justice Sotomayor that we should avoid giving the United States an undue hold-up, but the minimalist and legitimacy-preserving course is to deny entry as proposed and invite either a truly severable State-only decree that neither dismisses nor prejudices federal claims nor constrains federal operations, or a global settlement including federal consent. The McCarran Amendment and §1251(b)(2) may provide alternative fora for U.S.–State disputes, but they do not supply the clear authorization to approve a decree here that functionally binds the federal sovereign over its objection.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s reliance on Firefighters v. Cleveland is the strongest objection, but it does not defeat entry of a decree that—by its text—resolves only the Compact parties’ obligations inter se and expressly neither binds nor prejudices the United States, whose claims are dismissed without prejudice. Firefighters forbids using consent to bind a nonconsenting party; it does not require us to reject a state–state settlement in our exclusive § 1251(a) jurisdiction merely because the United States asserts parallel interests, especially where any federal reclamation-operational dispute can proceed under § 1251(b)(2) (and, where applicable, the McCarran Amendment) without being precluded. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers concerns rightly caution against a decree that manages federal project operations, but that is a tailoring problem, not a veto power: we can cabin the decree to state compliance without adjudicating federal duties. Texas v. New Mexico (2018) recognizes federal intervention to protect cognizable interests, yet it does not transform that intervention into authority to block the States from settling the only forum Congress made exclusive for their controversy.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to stress §1251(a)’s exclusivity for the State–State controversy, but that jurisdictional grant does not supply affirmative authority to enter a decree that disposes of a nonconsenting party’s claims in the very case where it has intervened. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, Firefighters v. Cleveland draws a categorical line: a consent decree cannot extinguish or practically burden a nonconsenting intervenor, and “without prejudice” does not cure a settlement that locks in operational baselines and thereby constrains the United States’ asserted Rio Grande Project interests recognized as cognizable in Texas v. New Mexico (2018). Justice Sotomayor’s pragmatism about allowing States to settle is appealing, but under a textualist, consequence-aware approach the better institutional course is to require either federal consent or a decree pared back so it neither dismisses nor functionally prejudices federal claims or operational discretion. The McCarran Amendment remains too limited a waiver to justify binding (even effectively) the federal sovereign through a state-negotiated decree over federal objection.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s reliance on Firefighters v. Cleveland is the most serious obstacle, but I do not read Firefighters to require us to deny all State–State settlements simply because a nonconsenting intervenor is present; it forbids binding or extinguishing that intervenor’s claims. I agree with Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh that the workable line is a decree narrowly limited to State–State obligations that neither dismisses the United States nor purports to set operational baselines for the Rio Grande Project, thereby avoiding any functional preclusion of federal positions. On the structure Congress created—§ 1251(a) exclusivity for State–State disputes and § 1251(b)(2)’s preservation of alternative forums for U.S.–State disputes—refusing any enforceable State-only resolution effectively hands the United States a veto over the only forum the States have, with serious real-world harms for downstream communities. Texas v. New Mexico (2018) rightly recognizes cognizable federal interests, but it does not require freezing the States’ ability to secure compliance between themselves when we can cabin the decree to preserve federal rights fully.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to emphasize §1251(a)’s exclusivity and the practical need to let States settle their compact dispute, but Firefighters v. Cleveland still limits what we may enter as a “consent decree” when a party before the Court—the United States—objects: we cannot approve a decree that dismisses its claims or functionally constrains its asserted interests merely by labeling the dismissal “without prejudice.” As the Chief Justice notes, the operative baselines the settlement would lock in can, as a practical matter, prejudice the United States’ Rio Grande Project positions—exactly the kind of functional binding Firefighters warns against. Texas v. New Mexico (2018), cited by several colleagues, cuts against Thomas because it recognizes the United States’ cognizable compact-related and reclamation interests, making it harder to treat federal objections as collateral to the very controversy we are asked to decree. I agree with Justice Sotomayor’s workability concern, but the pragmatic middle ground is to deny entry as proposed and invite a decree truly severable from (and nonprejudicial to) federal claims unless and until the United States consents.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to stress § 1251(a)’s exclusivity for State–State controversies and the risk of giving the United States a practical veto over settlement, but that does not answer the Firefighters v. Cleveland problem Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan identify: we lack authority to enter a “consent” decree that, in this very action, dismisses or functionally compromises a nonconsenting intervenor’s live claims. Even if styled “without prejudice,” the decree’s operational baselines can effectively bind the United States’ asserted Rio Grande Project interests recognized as cognizable in Texas v. New Mexico (2018), creating real-world preclusion and separation-of-powers concerns absent a clear congressional statement. Justice Sotomayor’s workability point is serious, yet the workable, text-and-precedent-consistent path is to require a decree truly severable from federal claims (no dismissal, no constraint, no prejudice) or to deny entry as proposed and invite a global settlement including the United States.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that Article III and § 1251(a) make this an exclusive forum for State–State disputes, and I share the concern (echoed by Justice Sotomayor) about not giving the United States an effective veto over interstate settlements. But Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s Firefighters v. Cleveland point remains dispositive for me: even if labeled “without prejudice,” a decree that dismisses a nonconsenting intervenor’s live claims in this very case—or that operationally locks in baselines that functionally constrain Reclamation—exceeds what a consent decree may do absent consent. Texas v. New Mexico (2018) matters because it recognizes the United States has cognizable reclamation/project interests intertwined with the Compact dispute here, which heightens the risk that the proposed decree would practically bind federal operations or litigation positions. Institutionally and as a matter of precedent, the correct course is to deny entry as proposed and invite a genuinely state-only decree that neither dismisses nor prejudices federal claims (or a global settlement including the United States).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that Article III and 28 U.S.C. § 1251(a) make this Court the exclusive forum for the States’ compact controversy, and I agree we should not let federal intervention become a de facto veto over a state–state settlement. But Firefighters v. Cleveland, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, is a constraint on our remedial power: we cannot enter a “consent” decree that dismisses or functionally impairs the United States’ asserted claims while it remains a nonconsenting party in this case, even if labeled “without prejudice.” Texas v. New Mexico (2018) matters because it recognizes the United States’ participation here as cognizable at least where its interests overlap with compact enforcement and project operations; that makes it difficult to say the federal objections are purely collateral or safely relegated to other forums. Textually and institutionally, the proper course is to deny approval as structured (or require narrowing) so the decree resolves only state–state obligations without prejudicing, constraining, or dismissing federal claims absent federal consent or adjudication.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that §1251(a) reflects a structural commitment to letting States resolve their exclusive-jurisdiction disputes without a federal veto, and that a decree textually limited to State–State duties is not automatically an “obligation” on the United States. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Firefighters v. Cleveland is a procedural-fairness backstop: we cannot enter a consent decree that, in operation, disposes of a nonconsenting party’s live claims or locks in baselines that functionally constrain that party’s litigation and operational positions. Texas v. New Mexico (2018) matters because it confirms the United States’ asserted project-operation interests are cognizable here, making “dismissal without prejudice” inadequate if the settlement’s terms effectively pre-judge or cabin those interests. The pragmatic, workable course is to allow only a clearly severable State–State decree that neither dismisses nor prejudices federal claims (and does not indirectly regulate Reclamation operations) absent federal consent or adjudication.

John Roberts.reasoning: We may not enter a consent decree that disposes of the claims of a nonconsenting intervenor or imposes obligations on that nonconsenting party. Firefighters v. Cleveland makes clear that a court’s approval of a settlement “cannot dispose of the valid claims of nonconsenting intervenors” and may not “impose[] obligations on a party that did not consent,” and the United States has not consented to dismissal of its asserted Compact-related claims or to decree terms constraining Rio Grande Project operations. Given the Compact’s federal approval (Act of May 31, 1939) and the Court’s prior recognition in Texas v. New Mexico (2018) that the United States may litigate to protect federal reclamation interests, institutional legitimacy and minimalism counsel denying entry as proposed and requiring any decree either to secure federal consent or to be narrowed to avoid binding the United States. The appropriate course is to avoid a decree that effectively alters federal project administration without the United States’ agreement, consistent with Article III original-jurisdiction practice and 28 U.S.C. § 1251.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III and 28 U.S.C. § 1251(a) give this Court exclusive original jurisdiction over controversies between States, so the Court should respect and enforce a States’ consent decree that resolves the Compact dispute on its terms without rewriting the Compact or importing extra-textual federal conditions. The United States’ participation is not required to settle an interstate controversy, and its asserted interests can be pursued elsewhere because suits between the United States and a State fall within this Court’s nonexclusive original jurisdiction, § 1251(b)(2), and the McCarran Amendment, 43 U.S.C. § 666, provides a forum for federal claims in state adjudications. Nothing in the Rio Grande Compact’s text or the Constitution authorizes using a State–State decree to impose new obligations on, or constraints upon, federal reclamation operations absent the United States’ consent; dismissing the United States’ claims without prejudice preserves its ability to litigate those theories in proper fora. Consistent with Texas v. New Mexico, 583 U.S. 407 (2018), any federal intervention must be limited and cannot be used to distort the States’ bargain or convert the Compact case into a broader federal project-management suit.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: A consent decree is, by definition, a product of the parties’ consent and therefore cannot bind a nonconsenting intervenor or dispose of its asserted claims; this Court has recognized that principle in Firefighters v. Cleveland. Because the United States intervened to assert interests tied to the Rio Grande Project and federal reclamation operations, approving a decree that dismisses the United States’ claims or constrains Project administration without federal consent would conflict with that settled limitation and risk practical interference with federal operations under the Reclamation Act framework. Nothing in Article III or 28 U.S.C. § 1251 authorizes using original jurisdiction to impose new obligations on the federal government by “settlement” when it withholds consent, and the McCarran Amendment’s waiver is limited and does not convert the United States into a party whose claims can be extinguished by others’ agreement. The proper course is to deny entry of a decree that purports to settle the federal controversies without the United States’ assent and instead require either an adjudication or a global settlement including all parties with asserted interests.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I would approve the Texas–New Mexico consent decree insofar as it resolves the States’ Compact dispute and dismisses the United States’ claims without prejudice, because Article III and 28 U.S.C. § 1251(a) make this Court the exclusive forum for interstate controversies, while 28 U.S.C. § 1251(b)(2) preserves alternative forums for United States–State disputes. As Texas v. New Mexico, 583 U.S. 407 (2018), reflects, the United States may participate to protect distinct federal interests, but a State-to-State settlement that does not impose new obligations on or constrain federal reclamation operations can be entered without forcing federal consent, particularly where the United States remains free to litigate elsewhere under the McCarran Amendment, 43 U.S.C. § 666. Pragmatically, denying approval would prolong a highly asymmetric dispute and risk real-world harm to downstream communities dependent on reliable deliveries, while approval provides enforceable relief between the States without prejudicing federal claims. The decree’s careful avoidance of terms that bind Reclamation without consent appropriately respects sovereign immunity while still securing equitable, workable compliance with the Rio Grande Compact.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: A consent decree is a creature of party agreement, and under Firefighters v. Cleveland it cannot dispose of the valid claims of a nonconsenting party or impose obligations on that party without consent. Because the United States is a party in this original action (Art. III, § 2; 28 U.S.C. § 1251) and asserts interests tied to the Rio Grande Project under federal reclamation law (Reclamation Act of 1902) and related contractual/project-operation authorities, the Court should not approve a decree that would dismiss or compromise those asserted federal claims over the United States’ objection. Workability and statutory coherence favor allowing the States to settle their interstate allocation issues, but only on terms that either (a) secure federal consent or (b) are clearly limited so they do not bind, constrain, or prejudice the United States’ distinct claims—especially given this Court’s prior recognition that the federal government may have cognizable interests in Compact administration in Texas v. New Mexico (2018).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III and 28 U.S.C. § 1251 authorize this Court to resolve the interstate Compact controversy, but they do not empower us to enter a decree that extinguishes the United States’ asserted federal interests without its consent; absent clear congressional authorization, courts should not imply constraints on federal reclamation operations or federal rights beyond what Congress has provided. Our decision in Texas v. New Mexico, 583 U.S. 407 (2018), allowed federal intervention only to pursue Compact claims that are “essentially the same” as Texas’s, not to be involuntarily dismissed or bound by a state-negotiated settlement. The McCarran Amendment, 43 U.S.C. § 666, reflects a policy against piecemeal water-rights adjudication, but it is a limited waiver of sovereign immunity and cannot be read to authorize binding or preclusive relief against the United States in this original action without its agreement. Consistent with separation-of-powers principles and the clear-statement approach reflected in United States v. New Mexico, 464 U.S. 528 (1984), the Court should not approve a consent decree that resolves the States’ dispute only by dismissing the United States’ claims over its objection.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Court should approve a Texas–New Mexico consent decree only to the extent it resolves the States’ interstate Compact controversy, but it cannot dismiss or otherwise dispose of the United States’ asserted claims, or impose operational constraints on federal reclamation/project operations, without the United States’ consent. Under Local No. 93, Int’l Ass’n of Firefighters v. City of Cleveland, a consent decree cannot compromise the valid claims of a nonconsenting intervenor, and Article III/28 U.S.C. § 1251 do not authorize using original jurisdiction to bind the federal government beyond what it has agreed to. Consistent with Texas v. New Mexico (2018), the United States may participate to protect distinct federal interests in the Rio Grande Project under the Reclamation Act framework, and any decree must avoid creating new federal obligations or foreclosing federal claims absent consent. Practical workability and institutional legitimacy counsel adopting a decree that settles the States’ dispute while preserving the United States’ ability to litigate any remaining federal claims in an appropriate forum (including under the McCarran Amendment, 43 U.S.C. § 666).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article III and 28 U.S.C. § 1251 authorize this Court to resolve the interstate Compact controversy, but they do not permit entry of a “consent decree” that effectively disposes of the United States’ asserted claims or imposes operational constraints on federal reclamation/project operations absent the United States’ consent or a clear waiver of sovereign immunity. The Rio Grande Compact (53 Stat. 785) defines the Compact Commission’s limited functions, and this Court has held that a decree in an original-jurisdiction compact case cannot expand or modify compact-created powers. See Texas v. New Mexico, 462 U.S. 554, 564–565 (1983). Although the McCarran Amendment, 43 U.S.C. § 666, waives immunity for certain comprehensive state water-rights adjudications, it does not license the Court to bind the United States through a state-to-state settlement that the United States has not joined; methodological consistency and precedent therefore counsel denying approval of the proposed decree as structured.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Even in our original jurisdiction, the Court cannot approve a consent decree that effectively disposes of a nonconsenting party’s asserted claims or imposes obligations on that party; the United States’ exceptions invoke the settled principle that “a court’s approval of a consent decree between some of the parties cannot dispose of the valid claims of nonconsenting intervenors,” Firefighters v. Cleveland, 478 U.S. 501, 529 (1986). Because the United States has appeared and asserted interests tied to federal reclamation/project operations under the Reclamation Act of 1902 and related federal contracts, approving a decree that dismisses its claims or functionally constrains federal operations without consent would raise serious procedural-fairness and practical-consequences concerns. Article III and 28 U.S.C. § 1251 authorize adjudication of the interstate dispute, but they do not license settlement terms that bind the federal sovereign absent consent, and nothing in Texas v. New Mexico (2018) authorizes extinguishing the United States’ claims via a State-only compact settlement. The appropriate course is to deny entry (or require modification) of any decree that purports to resolve or prejudice the United States’ claims without its consent, while allowing the States to settle their dispute only to the extent it does not bind or constrain the federal government.
